attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. He is reporting events, not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps Altman's Senate statement and 'his team' doing the lobbying behind the scenes. It is a historical observation with two parts.

contract.note: Reading 'stood next to me' as appearing at the same hearing, and 'water down' as pushing for narrower obligations, is an ordinary reading. Allowing the 2022 lobbying to come before the hearing matches the words, which give no order.

evidence.note: Official hearing transcript, 16 May 2023. Altman backs licensing and says he would be 'enthusiastic' about an oversight agency. Marcus takes part in the same exchange.
TIME report based on OpenAI's September 2022 white paper, sent privately to EU officials. It argued its general-purpose systems should not be classed as high risk, i.e. for fewer obligations.

reviews.rationale: Both parts hold. The hearing record shows Altman, alongside Marcus, endorsing licensing and an oversight agency. Documentary reporting shows OpenAI privately pushing to keep its systems out of the high-risk category, which means fewer obligations. OpenAI's reply that it supports safe regulation does not change the lobbying record.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Dropping 'like' narrows the claim to OpenAI, which is the example he names. Otherwise faithful. It is an observation about past conduct.

contract.note: Marcus names no promise or measure. Reading this as a material shortfall in promised safety resources is fair. But the result turns on the evaluator choosing the Superalignment pledge, and that pledge has a four-year window with no yearly schedule.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement: 20% of compute secured to date, spread over four years. It sets no amount due by August 2024.
Leike's firsthand account of struggling for compute. It is personal testimony, labelled as a company disclosure, and it does not measure delivery against the pledge.
WIRED, May 2024: the team was dissolved and its work absorbed elsewhere, as the company confirms. Dissolving the team does not measure what was delivered against the pledge.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows a public compute pledge and insider testimony about shortages, but no record of what was due by 20 August 2024 or what was actually delivered. The contract asks for a material shortfall against what was due. The pledge runs four years with no schedule, so the evidence does not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. Citing the former employees backs up his point; it does not make this their claim.

semantics.note: Faithful. The checkable parts are that the bill contains whistleblower protections and that former OpenAI staff called for them. 'Important' and 'critical' are value judgments.

contract.note: Fair, ordinary reading. It does not require the employees to have endorsed SB-1047 itself.

evidence.note: Official legislative analysis of the 19 August 2024 version, dated just before the post. It confirms the bill provides whistleblower protections.
'Right to Warn' letter, 4 June 2024, signed by several former OpenAI employees. It calls for protection against retaliation and says ordinary whistleblower protections are not enough.

reviews.rationale: The August version of the bill contained whistleblower protections, per the official analysis. Several former OpenAI employees publicly argued that such protections were needed. Both parts of the contract's support condition are met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own conclusion. It follows his quote from Veliz but is stated in his own words.

semantics.note: Keeps 'in the new form', 'basically only', and the wording about obvious negligence. It is an observation about the amended bill.

contract.note: Fair overall. 'Basically' allows minor exceptions, but a kept power to act before harm when there is an imminent threat is real preventive enforcement. That differs from 'only after something really bad happens'.

evidence.note: The sponsor's official description of the 15 August amendments. Civil penalties are cut unless harm has occurred or there is an imminent threat to public safety, so pre-harm enforcement is narrowed but not removed. The sponsor is an interested party.

reviews.rationale: The amendments narrowed pre-harm enforcement, which matches Marcus's general point. But the AG can still seek penalties before harm when public safety faces an imminent threat. That meets the contract's contradiction condition, against the claim that the bill can basically only be used after harm and no longer protects against dangerous negligence.
